questions.title: What decides a transmitter's excitatory or inhibitory action
questions.question: The excitatory or inhibitory action of a neurotransmitter is determined by which of the following?

options.A: The function of its postsynaptic receptor
options.C: The shape of the synaptic vesicle in which it is contained
options.D: The distance between the pre- and post-synaptic membranes

explanations.A: Correct. Whether a transmitter excites or inhibits the postsynaptic cell is set not by the transmitter itself but by the receptor (and the ion channel it gates) on the postsynaptic membrane. The same transmitter can do either job depending on the receptor: acetylcholine excites at nicotinic receptors of skeletal muscle yet slows the heart through muscarinic (M2) receptors, and glutamate is generally excitatory while GABA is inhibitory because of the channels their receptors open. A receptor that opens Na+ (or Ca2+) channels produces an EPSP; one that opens Cl-/K+ channels produces an IPSP.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The molecular structure of the transmitter determines which receptors it can bind, but it does not by itself dictate an excitatory versus inhibitory outcome — the same molecule can be either, depending on the postsynaptic receptor engaged.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Vesicle shape/size relates to how transmitter is packaged and released, not to whether the postsynaptic response is excitatory or inhibitory.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The synaptic cleft width (~20 nm) affects diffusion time but not the sign of the response; excitation versus inhibition is decided at the postsynaptic receptor.

questions.learning_objective: State that whether a neurotransmitter is excitatory or inhibitory is determined by its postsynaptic receptor (and the ion channel it gates), not by the transmitter molecule itself.

questions.title: How synaptic transmission is terminated
questions.question: Synaptic transmission is terminated by which of the following?

options.B: Elevation of Ca2+ in the presynaptic knobs
options.C: Reuptake of neurotransmitter by the postsynaptic neuron
options.D: Degradation of neurotransmitter by specific enzymes

explanations.A: Incorrect. Blocking the postsynaptic receptor (as a drug/toxin might) prevents a response, but it is not the physiological mechanism that clears released transmitter and ends normal synaptic signalling.
explanations.B: Incorrect. A rise in presynaptic Ca2+ triggers and sustains transmitter RELEASE (and underlies post-tetanic potentiation); it starts transmission rather than terminating it.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Reuptake does terminate signalling for many transmitters, but it is carried out by the PRESYNAPTIC terminal (and neighbouring glia) via membrane transporters — not by the postsynaptic neuron, so this option is wrong as stated.
explanations.D: Correct. Once released, transmitter action is ended by three routes: enzymatic degradation, reuptake into the presynaptic terminal/glia, and simple diffusion out of the cleft. Enzymatic degradation is the option that is correct here — the classic example is acetylcholinesterase, which hydrolyses acetylcholine in the cleft (monoamine oxidase and catechol-O-methyltransferase play the analogous role for monoamines). Rapid removal is what restores the synapse for the next signal and prevents continuous receptor activation.

questions.learning_objective: Identify enzymatic degradation (e.g. acetylcholinesterase) as a mechanism terminating synaptic transmission, and recognise that reuptake is presynaptic (not postsynaptic).

questions.title: Strychnine does not depress synaptic transmission
questions.question: Synaptic depression may result from all of the following EXCEPT:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Botulinum toxin blocks the release of acetylcholine at the neuromuscular junction, depressing transmission and causing flaccid paralysis — so it does depress the synapse.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Synaptic transmission is highly energy-dependent, so hypoxia depresses it (transmitter synthesis and release fail without adequate oxygen).
explanations.C: Incorrect. Acidosis depresses neuronal excitability and synaptic transmission (whereas alkalosis increases excitability), so it too is a cause of synaptic depression.
explanations.D: Correct. Strychnine does NOT depress synaptic transmission — it is a competitive antagonist at the inhibitory GLYCINE receptor. By removing postsynaptic glycine-mediated inhibition (especially the Renshaw-cell recurrent inhibition of spinal motor neurons), it produces DISINHIBITION with heightened excitability and convulsions, the opposite of depression. It is the exception in a list of synaptic depressants.

questions.learning_objective: Recognise strychnine as a glycine-receptor antagonist that causes excitation/convulsions by disinhibition, so it does not depress synaptic transmission (unlike botulinum toxin, hypoxia and acidosis).

questions.title: Properties of the Renshaw cell
questions.question: Regarding the Renshaw cell:

options.B: It shows the phenomenon of negative feedback inhibition
options.C: It is present in the dorsal horn of the spinal cord

explanations.A: Incorrect. The Renshaw cell is activated by ACETYLCHOLINE released from recurrent collaterals of the alpha motor neuron; glycine is the transmitter it RELEASES onto the motor neuron, not the one that activates it.
explanations.B: Correct. The Renshaw cell mediates recurrent (feedback) inhibition: an alpha motor neuron sends a collateral back onto the Renshaw cell, which then inhibits that same (and neighbouring) motor neurons. Because the motor neuron thus limits its own firing, this is a classic negative-feedback loop that stabilises and smooths motor output.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Renshaw cells lie in the VENTRAL (anterior) horn of the spinal cord, alongside the motor neurons they regulate — not in the dorsal horn (which handles sensory input).
explanations.D: Incorrect. The Renshaw cell is an INHIBITORY interneuron; it releases glycine (an inhibitory transmitter), so it is not excitatory.

questions.learning_objective: Describe the Renshaw cell as a ventral-horn inhibitory interneuron, activated by acetylcholine from motor-neuron collaterals and releasing glycine, that mediates recurrent (negative-feedback) inhibition of motor neurons.

questions.title: Where visceral (referred) pain is felt
questions.question: Visceral pain is usually felt:

options.A: Deeply in the diseased viscus itself
options.B: In deep tissues close to the diseased viscus
options.C: In the skin area that just overlies the diseased viscus
options.D: In the skin area that shares the same dorsal root (dermatome) as the diseased viscus

explanations.A: Incorrect. Visceral pain is characteristically poorly localised and is usually NOT felt accurately in the viscus itself; the viscera have few nociceptors and sparse localisation cues.
explanations.B: Incorrect. It is not felt simply in the deep tissues adjacent to the organ; the referral follows a segmental (dermatomal) rule rather than mere proximity.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Referred pain is not felt in the skin directly overlying the organ but in the dermatome sharing the organ's spinal segment — which may be some distance from the viscus (e.g. cardiac pain to the left arm).
explanations.D: Correct. Visceral pain is typically REFERRED: the visceral afferents enter the cord at a given segment and converge with somatic afferents from the dermatome supplied by the same dorsal root, so the brain projects the pain to that body-surface dermatome. This convergence-projection rule is why diaphragmatic irritation refers to the shoulder (C3-5) and cardiac ischaemia to the left chest and arm (T1-4) — the skin of the same dorsal-root segment, not the skin overlying the organ.

questions.learning_objective: State that visceral pain is referred to the skin dermatome sharing the same dorsal root as the viscus (convergence-projection), not to the skin overlying the organ.

questions.title: Pain-sensitive intracranial structures
questions.question: Intracranial headache could result from injurious stimuli on all the following EXCEPT:

options.C: The wall of the large intracranial veins (venous sinuses)

explanations.A: Incorrect. The dura mater (especially at the base of the skull) is pain-sensitive; traction or inflammation of the dura is a genuine source of intracranial headache.
explanations.B: Correct. The brain PARENCHYMA itself is insensitive to pain — it contains no nociceptors, which is why brain tissue can be cut or stimulated in awake neurosurgery without pain. Intracranial headache instead arises from the pain-sensitive structures around the brain (dura, large venous sinuses and their tributary veins, the dural/meningeal arteries and the large arteries at the base, and certain cranial nerves). Therefore the brain tissue is the exception.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The large intracranial (dural venous) sinuses and the big veins draining into them are pain-sensitive; traction on them causes headache.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The middle meningeal artery and the other dural/basal arteries are pain-sensitive; their dilatation or irritation produces headache.

questions.learning_objective: State that the brain parenchyma is insensitive to pain and that intracranial headache arises from pain-sensitive structures (dura, large venous sinuses/veins, meningeal and basal arteries).
